newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS- Iraq, U.N. agree cut in oil contract prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Iraq, U.N. agree cut in oil contract prices.

text.p: Iraq late Tuesday turned over to U.N.-appointed overseers a pricing formula for August oil sales, reducing prices for Basrah Light and Kirkuk crudes after initial objections from the U.N. experts.

The move by Baghdad sets the stage for final implementation of second round "oil-for-food" accord sales, barring any last minute objections from the U.N. Sanctions Committee in the next two days, diplomats said.

Oil trade sources and diplomats said the overseers and Iraqi State Oil and Marketing (SOMO) officials held a one-hour phone call earlier Tuesday. The discussion resulted in Baghdad agreeing to reduce its expectations for oil price formula contracts, sources said.
Basrah Light to the U.S. is now priced at $4.50 under West Texas Intermediate for August on an FOB basis. Kirkuk to Europe is at Dated Brent -$1.90, and at WTI -$3.50 for the U.S.
Asian customers received a price for Basrah Light at an average of Oman/Dubai -55 cents, sources said, also on an FOB basis for August.

Earlier in the day, SOMO had proposed a price of $4.40 per barrel under regional benchmark WTI for U.S. buyers of its Basrah Light, according to traders with oil companies which had contracts in the first round of the deal.

That was up from a discount of $4.60 in May, when crude was last lifted from Mina al Bakr in the Middle East Gulf, and in line with the 20 cents rise in Saudi Arabian Light crude, which SOMO had been tracking in the first round.

Before Iraq resubmitted its price plan, oil traders said that the price was too high, given a rise in freight costs in the past two months and the difficulty in marketing a potentially hefty amount of Iraqi crude oil.
"It can't be sold at those numbers. Since the last time Iraqi oil was lifted, the freight costs have gone up 60 cents per barrel," said a trader with a company expecting to renew its contract.
"Iraq is talking $4.40 under WTI. But we want to see that adjusted to reflect the freight and the Saudi increase," said the trader.
Another Gulf Coast trader who deals with SOMO said he thought the Iraqis could find a market for one million barrels per day (bpd) of crude, depending on the price.
"I think they'll sell what there's a market for," he said. "It depends on the market's view of the price. If the market views it as adequate, they could pump even harder."
U.N. overseers are expected to formally submit the prices, with their recommendation, to the Security Council's sanctions committee on Iraq sometime Wednesday morning, diplomats said.
The committee then has 48 hours, the equivalent of two working days, to raise any objections to the formula or it automatically becomes valid.
Iraq's price submission was being informally reviewed by committee members late Tuesday.

Under terms of the accord, Iraq is allowed to sell up to $2.14 billion worth of crude over 180 days, starting from June 8, mainly to buy food and medicine for civilians suffering under sanctions imposed after the invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
-Patrick Connole, Tony McAuley, NY Oil Desk, 1 212 859 1620
